intro_en:
This segment of the Israel National Trail begins with a climb up Har Timna; from the summit there are fine views over the Timna Valley and the cliff walls surrounding it. After descending the mountain southwards, we reach the tourist area of the park around an artificial lake. The Israel National Trail leaves the Timna basin southwards and passes modern copper-mining quarries on its way to Nahal Raham and Be'er Ora.

 Be'er Milhan - Timna (52)
 Be'er Ora - Shehoret Canyon (54)
character_en: A fairly steep climb and descent of about 250 metres in elevation up to Har Timna. On the rest of the route, walking on easy, flat tracks or with gentle ascents and descents
transport_en: At the starting point: a bus stop on the Arava Road, 3 km from the visitor centre. During the park's opening hours there is a good chance of hitching a ride to the park entrance
pois_en: Har Timna. The artificial lake (tourist area)
important_en: The village of Be'er Ora is about 2.5 km from the end point and is reached on foot along a jeep track. In Be'er Ora you can stock up on food at the minimarket, and to its west there is a hikers' campsite.
description_en:
The Israel National Trail heads south from the Timna Park visitor centre, where there is water and toilets, and where it is possible to sleep nearby.
The trail enters the channel of Nahal Alakson (Diagonal Stream), which got its popular name from its diagonal shape on the map. Heat-loving desert plant species grow in the channel, among them several twisted acacia trees.
The channel cuts into ancient magmatic basement rocks. Further up the trail we also meet the younger sedimentary sandstone rocks, deposited on top of the older basement rocks. After the uplift of Har Timna, weathering processes stripped the sandstone layer from large areas of the mountain. Dark lines can be seen on the basement rocks: these are the dykes, magmatic intrusive rocks. Magma that penetrated into cracks and lines of weakness solidified inside them.
Further up the trail, we also pass a "mushroom", a large sandstone rock standing on a stem. The forces of erosion sculpt the sandstone into unusual shapes. From this point, the climb to the summit of Har Timna becomes steeper and more strenuous: about 250 metres of vertical height over a distance of about 3 km.
The summit of Har Timna is flat, in contrast to the jagged landscape we saw on the way up the mountain. From the summit there is a fine view in all four directions. To the east, in Jordanian territory beyond the Arava, are the Edom Mountains. To the south, west and north lie the Timna Valley and the cliffs surrounding it. Har Timna is about 450 metres above sea level, while the highest summit visible at the top of the cliffs to the west is Har Berekh, which rises to 850 metres. The average elevation within the Timna Valley is about 300 metres.
We descend from the mountain southwards, slowly and carefully. Over a kilometre of walking we lose about 200 metres of vertical height over a distance of about 1.5 km. The end of the steep descent is marked by an acacia tree that the trail passes.
From here, the trail continues into the Timna Valley on a gentle route along a stream channel. When we emerge with the channel into the wide valley, it is recommended to leave the Israel National Trail briefly and walk about 1 km to the Hathor Temple and Solomon's Pillars.
A green-marked dirt road turns right towards a nearby reddish-brown ridge; after a short walk we meet a blue-marked trail. We turn left and walk around the rock walls.
The Hathor Temple is surrounded by a fence with explanatory signs beside it. This is an Egyptian temple to the patron goddess of copper mining, and above it a rock engraving was discovered on a rock face showing King Ramesses presenting her with an offering. A well-made stepped path climbs between the sandstone cliffs, passes the engraving and descends west to Solomon's Pillars, tall and impressive sandstone pillars sculpted by nature.
The Timna Valley is also distinguished by unique human activity over long periods. The archaeological evidence of copper mining and smelting found here is among the oldest in the world, from about 7,000 years ago. Scattered across the valley is a system of ancient mining shafts and tunnels and the remains of furnaces used for smelting copper.
The Egyptians mined copper in the Timna Valley from the 14th century until the middle of the 12th century BCE, at the initiative of the rulers of Egypt at that time. Copper mining at Timna was carried out by a local workforce with professional expertise. The inhabitants of the region had accumulated experience in mining and working copper over many generations beforehand. At the foot of Solomon's Pillars is an Egyptian temple to the goddess Hathor, the patron goddess of copper mining. Above the temple, a rock engraving was discovered on a rock face showing King Ramesses presenting an offering to the goddess Hathor.
The Israel National Trail continues to Timna Lake, and from afar we can already make out the crowns of the palm trees planted around the artificial lake. Beside the lake are a restaurant, a snack bar, toilets and taps for filling drinking water.
Continuing south, the trail follows a dirt road leading out of the Timna Valley. Beside the road we can see spoil heaps and mining pits left in the area where the modern copper mine operated in the second half of the 20th century. The mine was closed because it was not economically viable. In the 21st century mining was renewed, but the company running the site ran into a crisis and it is unclear whether activity there will continue.
The trail passes beside a landfill, crosses the landfill's access road and continues south to the wide channel of Nahal Raham. Nahal Raham rises on Har Uziyahu, in the area of Road 12, the road along the western border with Egypt. The drainage basin of Nahal Raham extends from the cliffs enclosing the Timna Valley to the south as far as Har Hizkiyahu. Its general flow direction is from south-west to north-east, and at this point the stream channel turns east on its way to the Arava Valley.
In the middle of the large channel, a broad-crowned acacia tree invites a break. This tree also "hosts" the acacia strap flower (Plicosepalus acaciae), a semi-parasitic plant attached to its branches. The strap flower draws water and minerals from the tree but carries out photosynthesis on its own, and is therefore considered a semi-parasite. Its leaves are green and elliptical, and its red flowers are tube-shaped, with the stamens and the style protruding from them.
The Palestine sunbird, a small bird with a long beak, pollinates the strap flower. Birds also disperse the strap flower's juicy fruits. The seed inside the fruit is sticky, and when it sticks to a tree branch it germinates and sends roots into the conducting vessels of the tree, its host, from which it draws the water and minerals it needs.
The Israel National Trail completes its crossing of the wide Nahal Raham channel and hugs the eastern side of the channel. We walk about another kilometre along a dirt road to a junction of roads.
From the end point of the segment, you can leave the Israel National Trail and walk about 2.5 km along a jeep track towards the south-east to the village of Be'er Ora, which has a minimarket as well as a hikers' campsite located outside the village. From the Israel National Trail we turn left onto a black-marked road, and further on turn right onto a blue-marked road that leads to Be'er Ora.
Another option is to continue along the Israel National Trail for about another 2 km up Nahal Raham, to its confluence with Nahal Etek. Beside the confluence of the streams is an informal overnight campsite.
nearby_en: The sites of the Timna basin, with an admission fee. Detailed information at the Timna Valley visitor centre.
The Sasgon Dune, in the north-west of the Timna Valley, accessible by private car free of charge (hikers on segment 51 pass beside it).
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, trail-marking coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
